chapters.title: 11.1 Running Cypress in GitHub Actions / GitLab CI / Jenkins
chapters.overviewText: CI runs cypress run, not cypress open. The official GitHub Action (cypress-io/github-action) installs dependencies, caches Cypress, can start the app, wait-on a URL, and then run. GitLab and Jenkins do the same steps as shell. Parallelism is extra jobs or Cloud --parallel (9.8), not a browser matrix inside one step.
chapters.why: A green local App means nothing if PRs never run the suite. Interviewers often ask you to sketch the GitHub workflow — including start/wait-on, browser, and artifacts.
chapters.when: When the suite exists and you need a merge gate; when adding staging env vars (10.2); when splitting smoke vs nightly (10.1).

practical.scenario: Every pull request must run @smoke against a booted HRM stack; main runs the full suite nightly.
practical.pass: You use cypress-io/github-action with start, wait-on, browser chrome, and CYPRESS_grepTags=@smoke on PRs. You do not SSH into a laptop to click cypress open.
practical.fail: You commit node_modules, skip wait-on so Cypress visits before Next.js is up, or you call cypress open in CI.

chapters.customSummary:
- GitHub: cypress-io/github-action — install, cache, start, wait-on, run.
- Always cypress run; never cypress open on the runner.
- Boot the app (start: npm run start / wait-on http://localhost:3000) or point baseUrl at a deployed staging.
- GitLab/Jenkins: same commands in YAML/Groovy; Docker image from 11.2.
- Artifacts and Cloud record come in later chapters — first make a single job green.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## GitHub Actions — the pattern to memorize

```yaml
name: cypress-smoke
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cypress-io/github-action@v6
        with:
          browser: chrome
          start: npm run start
          wait-on: 'http://localhost:3000'
          spec: cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts
        env:
          CYPRESS_grepTags: '@smoke'
          CYPRESS_BASE_URL: 'http://localhost:3000'
          CYPRESS_apiUrl: 'http://localhost:4000'
```

What the action does: npm ci (or yarn), cache the Cypress binary, run `start` in the background, poll `wait-on` until the HRM UI responds, then `cypress run --browser chrome`. If you already deploy staging, drop `start`/`wait-on` and set `CYPRESS_BASE_URL` to staging (10.2) with secrets for users.

## GitLab CI

```yaml
cypress:
  image: cypress/browsers:latest
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run start & npx wait-on http://localhost:3000
    - npx cypress run --browser chrome
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - cypress/screenshots
      - cypress/videos
```

Same story: image with browsers (11.2), install, boot, run.

## Jenkins

A pipeline stage with the same shell, or a Docker agent `cypress/included` so `cypress` is on PATH. Inject credentials as masked env (`CYPRESS_`). Do not store `cypress.env.json` on the agent disk with prod passwords.

## Parallel and browsers

Two browsers = two jobs (or a matrix). Spec sharding = matrix of spec globs or Cloud `--parallel` (9.8, 11.3). One step cannot "run Chrome and Firefox in parallel inside Cypress."

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

Playwright's GitHub action / `npx playwright install --with-deps` is the cousin. Selenium needs drivers or a Grid — more moving parts. Cypress's official action is a genuine DX advantage; still pin action major versions.

Interview line: "I use `cypress-io/github-action` with `start` + `wait-on` + `browser: chrome`. CI is `cypress run`. Smoke is `CYPRESS_grepTags`."

chapters.title: 11.2 Docker Images for Cypress
chapters.overviewText: Official images: cypress/base (Node + OS deps, you install Cypress), cypress/browsers (base + Chrome/Firefox/Edge), cypress/included (browsers + the Cypress binary ready to cypress run). Pin a tag that matches your Cypress major. Mount the project; write screenshots/videos to a volume. Playwright has microsoft/playwright images; Selenium has standalone Chrome images — same idea, different contents.
chapters.why: CI 'Cypress failed to start' is usually a missing system library or a Chrome version mismatch. Using cypress/browsers instead of a random node:22 image is the boring fix.
chapters.when: GitLab/Jenkins Docker agents, local parity with CI, and when GitHub's ubuntu-latest Chrome drifts from your laptop.

practical.scenario: GitLab runners must run the HRM suite in Docker with Chrome, without installing Cypress globally on the host.
practical.pass: You pick cypress/browsers (or included) pinned to a version, npm ci inside the project mount, and cypress run --browser chrome.
practical.fail: You use node:alpine, skip dependencies, and wonder why Electron cannot launch.

chapters.customSummary:
- cypress/base = OS deps + Node; you npm install cypress.
- cypress/browsers = + preinstalled browsers — usual CI choice.
- cypress/included = + Cypress binary — useful for 'just run', watch version drift vs package.json.
- Pin tags; mount artifacts. Not a substitute for Appium images.
- Playwright/Selenium have their own official images — do not mix binaries casually.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Which image

| Image | Contains | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `cypress/base` | Node, Xvfb, libraries | You need a custom Node and will `npm ci` Cypress |
| `cypress/browsers` | base + Chrome/Firefox/Edge | **Default CI recommendation** |
| `cypress/included` | browsers + Cypress already installed | Quick jobs; keep the image tag aligned with `package.json` Cypress version |

```bash
docker run --rm -it -v $PWD:/e2e -w /e2e cypress/browsers:node-22.14.0-chrome-134.0.0
npm ci
npx cypress run --browser chrome
```

`cypress/included` can skip `npm ci`'s Cypress download **if** versions match. If `package.json` says Cypress 14 and the image bundled 13, you will get mysterious binary errors — pin both.

## Compose with the app

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    healthcheck: { test: ['CMD', 'curl', '-f', 'http://localhost:3000'], interval: 5s }
  e2e:
    image: cypress/browsers:node-22.14.0-chrome-134.0.0
    depends_on:
      web: { condition: service_healthy }
    working_dir: /e2e
    volumes: [ '.:/e2e' ]
    command: npx cypress run --browser chrome
    environment:
      CYPRESS_BASE_URL: http://web:3000
```

From the e2e container, localhost is not the web service — use the Compose DNS name.

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

`mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` includes browsers **and** WebKit. `selenium/standalone-chrome` is a Grid node. `cypress/browsers` still has **no first-class WebKit** (9.9). Native mobile is a different image/stack (Appium).

Interview line: "I use official `cypress/browsers` (or `included` with matching versions). Alpine Node images are how you get 'Cypress failed to start'."

chapters.title: 11.3 Cypress Cloud — Recorded Runs, Dashboards, Analytics
chapters.overviewText: Cypress Cloud is the paid dashboard: record a run with --record --key, upload videos/screenshots, see spec timing, flake history, and (with enough machines) intelligent --parallel spec assignment. It does not unlock cy.origin or CT. Open-source Cypress can already run tests; Cloud is orchestration and visibility (Part 0.1).
chapters.why: Procurement will ask what you are buying. The honest answer is historical load-balancing, hosted artifacts, and flake analytics — not a new assertion API.
chapters.when: When CI has three runners and naive shards are unbalanced, when you need a PR status check with a URL, and when comparing Cloud to Sorry Cypress/Currents (11.5).

practical.scenario: Leadership wants a link in the GitHub PR showing which leave spec failed, plus parallelization that does not require hand-maintained globs.
practical.pass: You set projectId, inject CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY, and cypress run --record --parallel --ci-build-id. You explain Cloud is not extra commands.
practical.fail: You tell them Cloud is required to run Cypress in CI at all.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cloud = record + dashboard + flake analytics + smart --parallel. Not extra test APIs.
- --record --key / CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY; projectId in config.
- --parallel requires record and a shared ci-build-id across machines (9.8).
- OSS already has local video/screenshot; Cloud hosts them and graphs history.
- Playwright Trace is a zip; Cloud Replay is hosted (9.12). Selenium vendors sell similar dashboards.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## What you configure

```js
export default defineConfig({
  projectId: 'abc123', // from the Cloud UI
  e2e: { /* ... */ },
});
```

```bash
npx cypress run --record --key "$CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY" --parallel --ci-build-id "$GITHUB_RUN_ID"
```

Never commit the record key. GitHub secret → env `CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY` (the action also accepts `record: true` + the secret). All parallel machines **must** share the same `ci-build-id` or Cloud treats them as separate runs and cannot balance specs (9.8).

## What you get

- A URL per run (paste into the PR).
- Spec duration history → **smarter shards** than folder globs.
- Flake detection across attempts (pairs with 9.13 / 10.3 — still fix the test).
- Hosted screenshots/videos/Test Replay depending on plan (9.12, 11.4).

## What you do not get

- WebKit, multi-tab, or a Trace Viewer zip.
- Permission to skip `wait-on` or `data-cy`.
- Extra assertions. Cloud is orchestration and visibility (Part 0.1).

## Privacy

Payroll videos are compensation data. Legal may forbid `--record` to Cypress.io. Then use 11.5 (Sorry Cypress / Currents) or no record + artifacts (11.8).

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

Playwright OSS already shards and ships `trace.zip` without a Cypress-like paywall for *balancing*. Selenium + Sauce/BrowserStack is the old vendor-dashboard model. Cypress Cloud is closer to "a dashboard that speaks Cypress spec files" plus flake UI. Do not tell a Playwright team they "need Cloud to see traces."

Interview line: "Cloud records runs and load-balances specs across machines. I can run 100% of Cypress without it. I pay when CI orchestration and hosted replay matter — not because the runner is incomplete."

chapters.title: 11.4 Cypress Cloud AI Features
chapters.overviewText: Any 'AI' in the Cypress ecosystem sits on Cloud (failure clustering, debug assistance, Test Replay insights) — not in npm install cypress. It is not Playwright Trace Viewer, not a self-healing replacement for data-cy, and not a reason to skip cy.origin. Treat vendor AI as a helper on recorded runs; keep assertions deterministic.
chapters.why: Sales decks will blur AI, Test Replay, and 'self-healing locators.' Hiring managers want to hear you separate marketing from the runner you can git clone.
chapters.when: When evaluating a Cloud plan that lists AI/debug features, and when someone wants AI-generated specs as the suite.

practical.scenario: A vendor demo auto-suggests a locator after a failure. You must decide if Bizlevate should rely on it.
practical.pass: You use Cloud Debug/Replay to inspect a recorded failure, you still fix locators and waits in code, and you do not accept AI-suggested CSS as the strategy.
practical.fail: You describe Cypress as having built-in AI self-healing like a magic Playwright Trace.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cloud AI/debug features require recorded runs and a plan — not the OSS runner.
- Test Replay / Debug ≠ Trace Viewer zip (9.12).
- AI-suggested locators are hints; data-cy remains the strategy.
- Generated tests still need review (flake, origin, tabs).
- Playwright and Selenium vendors ship their own AI add-ons — same skepticism.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## What is real vs adjacent

**Real, paid, Cypress-branded:** Cloud Test Replay / Debug (reconstruct a recorded run), analytics that group failures, and whatever "AI" assistant the current Cloud plan wraps around those artifacts. These need `--record`.

**Not real in OSS Cypress:** a Trace Viewer, self-healing `cy.get('.css-x7k')` that silently retargets, or an offline zip you open with `show-trace`.

If the feature is not reproducible from `cypress run` without a key, it is Cloud, not Cypress-the-test-runner.

## How to use it without lying to yourself

1. Record CI (11.3).
2. Open the failed run; watch Replay if you have it.
3. Fix the spec: intercept, `data-cy`, `cy.origin` args (9.1), isolation.
4. If an AI panel suggests a selector, treat it like Selector Playground — a guess, then apply Part 4 discipline.

Generated Studio / AI specs will not invent `{ args }` for Okta. Review like a junior PR.

## Versus Playwright and Selenium vendors

Playwright's OSS trace is already a powerful post-mortem **without** AI. mabl, Testim, and some Selenium clouds have sold "self-healing" for years; it trades determinism for magic. Cypress Cloud AI is in that product category. Appium device clouds also sell analytics — still not a substitute for `data-cy`.

Interview line: "Cloud AI is dashboard assistance on recorded runs. The runner has no Trace Viewer and no self-healing I would bet payroll on. Playwright traces and Selenium vendor videos are the cousins."

chapters.title: 11.5 Cypress Cloud Alternatives
chapters.overviewText: If you want a dashboard and parallel coordination without Cypress.io billing, the historical OSS answer is Sorry Cypress; the commercial successor from that lineage is Currents. You still run OSS Cypress; you point recording at another ingest URL. Other options: report-only (Mochawesome, 11.6) with no dashboard, or generic CI artifacts. Playwright does not need this as badly because traces and shards are OSS.
chapters.why: Not every company will send videos of payroll screens to a US SaaS. Knowing Sorry Cypress / Currents is the practical answer to 'we cannot use Cypress Cloud.'
chapters.when: When Cloud is blocked by procurement/privacy, when you only need HTML reports, and when comparing TCO to Playwright.

practical.scenario: Legal forbids Cypress Cloud. You still want a run history URL for the QA manager.
practical.pass: You name Sorry Cypress (self-host) or Currents as the record-protocol alternatives, or you fall back to Mochawesome + screenshot artifacts with no record key.
practical.fail: You pirate a Cloud key or claim OSS Cypress includes the dashboard.

chapters.customSummary:
- Sorry Cypress: OSS dashboard compatible with Cypress recording protocol (self-host).
- Currents: commercial successor/alternative in that ecosystem.
- You can skip recording entirely: Mochawesome + CI artifacts.
- Pointing record to a third party still needs privacy review (payroll PII in videos).
- Playwright OSS traces reduce the need for a Cypress-like Cloud.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Sorry Cypress

Sorry Cypress is the well-known **open-source** stand-in for the Cypress Dashboard: it implements the recording API so `cypress run --record` can talk to *your* server instead of Cypress.io. You host director/API/dashboard, set the env vars the project documents (typically a record key and API URL override).

Operational truth: you now own Mongo/storage/upgrade. For a small Bizlevate team, that cost can exceed Cloud. For a bank that cannot leave the VPC, it is justified.

## Currents

Currents.dev (and related commercial offerings from the same problem-space) sell a hosted dashboard that speaks Cypress recording, with parallelization helpers. Think "Cloud-shaped product not billed by Cypress.io." Always verify current protocol compatibility with *your* Cypress major before promising a migration weekend.

## When you should not record anywhere

Payroll videos contain compensation. If legal says no third party and you will not self-host, **do not `--record`**. Use 11.6 HTML reports + 11.8 artifacts on GitHub (retention 7 days, restrict who can download). `blackout` on screenshots (9.15).

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

Playwright: `trace.zip` + HTML reporter in OSS. Selenium: ReportPortal, Allure, vendor clouds. Cypress is the tool whose *best* timeline debugger is behind a dashboard — hence this alternatives chapter.

Interview line: "Cloud alternatives are Sorry Cypress (self-host) and Currents (hosted). Or no record at all — Mochawesome plus artifacts."

chapters.title: 11.6 Test Reporting
chapters.overviewText: Each Cypress spec runs in a separate Mocha process, so a naive 'reporter: mochawesome' overwrites the JSON every spec. The two-part Mochawesome pattern is: (1) write one JSON per spec into a folder, (2) mochawesome-merge + marge (or cypress-mochawesome-reporter, which wraps that pipeline). JUnit XML is for Jenkins. Cypress Cloud is a reporter of a different kind (11.3).
chapters.why: A CI job that prints 'All specs passed' with no HTML is unreadable for a non-engineer PM. The overwrite bug is a rite of passage — interviewers have seen empty reports.
chapters.when: When you need a shareable HTML report without Cloud, or a JUnit file for Jenkins gates.

practical.scenario: Jenkins must display a pass/fail trend and an HTML report for the full HRM suite after a parallel matrix.
practical.pass: You configure a per-spec JSON reporter, merge after all shards, and generate HTML. You do not set reporter: mochawesome once and trust the last spec's file.
practical.fail: You open a report that only contains the last spec file and ship it.

chapters.customSummary:
- Specs = separate Mocha runs ⇒ one reporter file gets overwritten unless you use a per-spec output dir.
- Mochawesome two-part: JSON per spec, then mochawesome-merge + report generator (marge).
- cypress-mochawesome-reporter packages that pipeline.
- JUnit XML for Jenkins; HTML for humans; Cloud for recorded analytics.
- Playwright HTML reporter is first-party; Cypress HTML is plugin territory.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Why a single mochawesome file lies

Cypress launches a new runner per spec file. Mocha's default reporter writes `mochawesome.json` then the next spec **overwrites** it. The HTML shows one spec. This is the two-part problem.

## Two-part plugin pipeline

Part 1 — **during the run**, each spec writes its own JSON:

```js
// cypress.config.ts
reporter: 'cypress-multi-reporters',
reporterOptions: {
  reporterEnabled: 'mochawesome',
  mochawesomeReporterOptions: {
    reportDir: 'cypress/results',
    overwrite: false,
    html: false,
    json: true,
  },
},
```

Part 2 — **after all specs (and after all parallel jobs download artifacts)**:

```bash
npx mochawesome-merge cypress/results/*.json > cypress/results/merged.json
npx marge cypress/results/merged.json --reportDir cypress/report --inline
```

`cypress-mochawesome-reporter` is a convenience plugin that wires this so you are not assembling multi-reporters by hand. Either path is valid; **both are two stages: emit JSON, then merge/generate**.

## Parallel jobs

Each GitHub shard uploads `cypress/results`. A final job downloads all, merges, publishes HTML. If you merge too early, you only report one shard.

## JUnit

`junit` reporter (or mocha-junit-reporter) for Jenkins "test result" trend. Same overwrite rule — unique files per spec, then a Jenkins glob.

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

Playwright: built-in HTML reporter + blob reports you merge with `playwright merge-reports` — same *shape* as Mochawesome two-part. Selenium: Allure, Extent, ReportNG. Cypress does not bundle a first-party HTML report comparable to Playwright's.

Interview line: "Mochawesome is two-part because each spec is a new Mocha. I write JSON per spec, merge, then marge. A single report file only contains the last spec."

chapters.title: 11.7 Logging & Error Handling
chapters.overviewText: cy.log writes to the Command Log — great in cypress open, easy to miss in CI stdout. cy.task runs in Node and can console.log on the server, write files, or hit a logger — that is what you want in GitHub Actions. Failures: failOnStatusCode, uncaught:exception, unhandled rejections. Do not swallow every app exception globally to keep CI green.
chapters.why: Payroll bugs show up as uncaught exceptions in the app. A support file that returns false from uncaught:exception hides them. Interviewers distinguish cy.log from cy.task immediately.
chapters.when: When CI logs are empty besides Mocha errors, when a third-party widget throws, and when you need to print an axe violation list (9.7).

practical.scenario: Axe violations and failed API seeds must appear in the GitHub job log, not only in the App Command Log.
practical.pass: You register cy.task('log') in setupNodeEvents that console.logs in Node, call it from tests, and you only ignore uncaught:exception for a named third-party script with a comment.
practical.fail: You cy.log the violations and return false from uncaught:exception for all errors.

chapters.customSummary:
- cy.log → Command Log (GUI). cy.task → Node process (CI stdout/files).
- Register tasks in setupNodeEvents; return a promise/value.
- uncaught:exception: returning false skips the fail — use narrowly.
- failOnStatusCode: false on cy.visit/request is opt-in, not default for happy paths.
- Playwright: test.info().attach / console in the Node test process — closer to cy.task than cy.log.

chapters.title: 11.8 Artifacts: Screenshots & Videos on Failure
chapters.overviewText: On cypress run, failed tests can write PNGs (screenshotOnRunFailure, still default true) and MP4s (video — default false since Cypress 13). Upload those folders as CI artifacts. They are not Trace Viewer. Blackout PII (9.15). Keep video on failure-only if your Cypress version supports it, or delete passing videos to save storage.
chapters.why: Without artifacts, a CI-only failure is a stack trace. With unbounded videos, the GitHub artifact budget explodes. Both are preventable.
chapters.when: The first green CI job, and when a PM asks for a recording of the failed payroll run.

practical.scenario: Failed specs on GitHub must attach screenshots; videos only when a test failed, without uploading 2GB of green runs.
practical.pass: You enable screenshotOnRunFailure, set video true (or retain-on-failure if available), upload cypress/screenshots and cypress/videos, and you know Cypress 13 changed the video default to false.
practical.fail: You assume videos always record, or you look for a trace.zip in the artifact zip.

chapters.customSummary:
- Screenshots on failure: on by default; folder cypress/screenshots.
- Videos: set video: true explicitly after Cypress 13; watch disk/CPU (12.4).
- Upload as GitHub/GitLab artifacts; not a Trace Viewer zip (9.12).
- Blackout payroll PII; restrict artifact access.
- Playwright: screenshot/video/trace are separate retain-on-failure flags — Cypress video is cruder.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Config

```js
export default defineConfig({
  screenshotOnRunFailure: true,
  screenshotsFolder: 'cypress/screenshots',
  video: true,
  videoCompression: 32,
  videosFolder: 'cypress/videos',
});
```

**Cypress 13:** `video` default became `false`. Tutorials that say "CI always has video" are stale. Set it if you want it.

If your version supports retaining videos only on failure, prefer that. Otherwise delete `cypress/videos` for passing specs in a CI step, or accept the storage bill.

## GitHub upload

```yaml
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  if: failure()
  with:
    name: cypress-artifacts
    path: |
      cypress/screenshots
      cypress/videos
```

`if: failure()` still uploads when the Cypress step failed *if* you place this step correctly (often `if: always()` after the test step so you get artifacts even when the job is red — use `always()` + a small retention).

## Not traces

A video is a camera pointed at the browser. You cannot click a command to restore DOM. Cloud Replay (11.3) is closer. Playwright `trace.zip` is closer still (9.12).

## Versus Playwright and Selenium

Playwright: `screenshot: 'only-on-failure'`, `video: 'retain-on-failure'`, `trace: 'retain-on-failure'` — three knobs. Selenium vendors: session video. Cypress: screenshot + optional video, plugin for visual diff (9.6).

Interview line: "I upload screenshots always-on-failure. I turn videos on explicitly because Cypress 13 defaulted them off. There is no trace.zip."
